what: The redness of the two-sitting stand that `pnpm run gate` admits, by name, with a ceiling and a date.

WHO ADMITTED IT, AND WHO HAS NOT. The orchestrator of step Ш6 did, on 2026-08-25, on its own authority and nobody else's. The owner has not seen this file, was not asked about it, and has agreed to none of it. That is what `ratifiedBy: null` on every line below means, and it means nothing weaker: not `unknown`, not `not applicable`, but the record that five red points are standing on one agent's decision, unreviewed. `tools/gate.mjs` prints it whenever the FULL gate reaches this budget at all, green or red, so that a green gate cannot be read as more than it is -- `gate:fast` never gets here, and neither does a run whose stand died before it judged. `tests/stand/allowance.ts` refuses a line that names the owner in `allowedBy` while `ratifiedBy` is null, because that is the exact sentence this file was first written with: all five lines said "owner, through the Ш6 orchestrator, 2026-08-25", and no owner had been asked. When the owner ratifies -- or refuses -- their name and the date go in `ratifiedBy`, and the line stops being one agent's word.

WHAT `null` DOES NOT MEAN. It does not mean the owner said no. There is no value of `ratifiedBy` for that, and there deliberately is not one: a line the owner has REFUSED is not an unreviewed permission, it is an overridden one, and it has no business standing in a budget. If the owner says no, the line is DELETED and the gate goes red -- that is the whole procedure. A union type distinguishing 'refused' from 'not asked' was considered and refused in turn: it would branch every place that reads the field and double the cases about it, for a state that has occurred nought times. So `null` is unambiguous, and it says one thing: nobody has been asked.

WHAT A RATIFICATION HAS TO CARRY. Not a name. A name alone was the quieter half of the same forgery: the gate says `allowedBy` out loud, so writing "owner" there is visible, while writing "owner" into `ratifiedBy` was silent AND switched off the check on `allowedBy` at the same time. So a non-null `ratifiedBy` has to carry a day, as YYYY-MM-DD, and a place a reader can go and look -- a commit id, a path, a file, a URL. Only the SHAPE is checked. Nothing here can tell whether the place says what the line claims, and nothing here pretends to; resolving the citation with `git cat-file -e` was weighed and dropped, because it costs the suite its ability to run on a tree without that history and forces every ratification to be a commit. Both halves are now printed by the gate.

HOW LONG AN UNRATIFIED LINE MAY LIVE. `expires` was the only pressure, and it presses on the LINE rather than on the owner -- while the date is moved by the same party that never asked, for free, as often as it likes. Nothing counted that, so `ratifiedBy: null` could survive for ever in fortnight steps, each step an ordinary-looking diff. `renewals` counts the moves, and the rule is one: unratified, a line may be extended ONCE; a second extension needs a name in `ratifiedBy`, or the point fixed and the line deleted. WHAT IT COSTS: the counter is written by hand and can be written down. What it buys is that an uncounted renewal is then a deliberate lie sitting in a diff, where the defect it replaces was forgetfulness.

NONE OF THIS IS A BOUNDARY, and a reader who does not know that will think the machinery is stronger than it is. Whoever can edit this file can edit `tests/stand/allowance.ts` in the same commit; every rule above is one deletion away from gone. These checks buy exactly one thing -- that the false sentence has to be written ON PURPOSE, and lands in a diff where somebody can see it. They cost nothing against a determined author and they were never meant to. The defect they were built for was carelessness: five lines saying the owner had agreed, written in one sitting because it was the easiest thing to type.

Why it exists. `pnpm run test:stand` exits 1 on this revision, and not because the stand is broken: the points below are red about the product, and they belong to steps that have not happened -- Ш7 (the restore traps) and Ш8 (the strip's queue and adoption). A gate that took the stand as it is would be red until those land, and a `pre-push` hook over a permanently red gate is a hook that comes off with the first `--no-verify`.

HOW MANY POINTS ARE RED depends on the run. Five points need a line: 3, 4, 6 and 7 came back red in every run measured, and point 1 came back GREEN in two of the six. So a run of the stand shows four or five of its nine points red, not five every time, and the fifth line is carrying an intermittent defect -- which is what `mayBeGreen` on that line is for.

So the redness is admitted here rather than ignored there, and the admission is held to five things a comment could not hold it to. A point that goes red without a line here is red. A point red by MORE than its `atMost` is red. A point that comes back GREEN is red -- take the line out -- unless its line carries `mayBeGreen: true`, which needs the runs behind it written into `seen`. Every line stops working on `expires`, whatever else is true. And `cap` is how many lines may live at once: a new one is written after an old one is taken out, not beside it.

`expires`, `cap`, `renewals` and the `allowedBy` / `ratifiedBy` pair are asserted by `tests/stand/allowance.test.ts`, which needs no editor and runs on every `npx jest`. That is the difference between a deadline and a note about one, and between a signature and a name somebody typed.

WHY A CEILING AND NOT AN EXACT NUMBER. The design this was built to was stricter: a point red by LESS than its line said was to be refused too, so that a budget nobody tightens could not quietly become a permission with no end. That rule presumes the stand's answer is a function of the product. It is not, and 2026-08-25 is the measurement -- runs of the stand on one revision with nothing changed between them:
run 6  02:20  .     .     .     1     1     .     3     3     .   <- still on disk

`.` is green. SIX IS A FLOOR, NOT A COUNT, and that is said here because this file first said five while a report of the same step said six. `tests/stand/run.mjs` deletes `.vscode-test/stand-output/` at the start of every run (`prepare()`), so a run's numbers survive exactly until the next run starts: rows 1 to 5 are transcribed from runs whose recordings no longer exist and cannot be re-read by anybody, here or later. Row 6 is the one that can be: it is `.vscode-test/stand-output/verdict.json` as it stands, left by the full gate whose receipt in `.gate/receipts.ndjson` is stamped 2026-08-25T00:20:13Z. That receipt file records FOUR gate-driven stand runs; a standalone `pnpm run test:stand` leaves no receipt at all, so the total is not established and no number here should be read as one.

Point 1 -- the accumulating editor groups, the defect the stand was built for -- came back green in two runs of six. Point 3 moved 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 1 and point 7 moved 3, 3, 3, 3, 2, 3, so BOTH directions of the exact rule fire on noise: run 5 would have been refused for being better at point 7, and runs 1 and 6 for being better at points 1 and 3. An exact number over a random variable is a coin, and a gate that is a coin teaches a person to run it again instead of reading it, which is the one thing the plan says a gate must never do. The plan's own Ш9 anticipates exactly this shape: 'if the miss is really one in ten, a green run is unreachable, and the rule has to be `the miss rate did not grow`'.

The exact rule is therefore kept where it is sound and named where it is not: a line whose `atMost` equals what the point always returns IS the exact rule, and `mayBeGreen` is the escape, per line, with its evidence beside it. The pressure to shrink rests on `expires` and `cap`, which are machine-enforced and need no reproducibility at all.

How to take a line out: fix the point, run `pnpm run gate`, delete the line. The gate refuses a line whose point is green unless the line admits green, so a fixed defect cannot leave its permission behind.

`atMost` is `Finding.violations` from `tests/stand/judge.ts` -- how many named things went wrong at that point, as an integer. It is not a physical magnitude and two points' numbers do not compare with each other; the magnitude a person needs is in `measured`, which nothing checks.

Read by the gate to decide a colour: `point`, `answer`, `atMost`, `mayBeGreen`, `expires`, `cap`, `renewals`. Read by the gate and printed on every full run: `allowedBy`, `ratifiedBy`, `renewals`. Read by people: `says`, `seen`, `measured`, `why`.
